title: Casimir forces on suspended thin dielectric membranes covered with graphene
authors: Tze Ue Ngai, Zuocheng Zhang, Q. Zhang, Youssef Jeyar, Jingwei Li, Zhengtang Luo, Mauro Antezza, H. B. Chan
abstract: We investigate the Casimir force on thin suspended dielectric layers covered with graphene, both theoretically and experimentally. Thermal effects of the Casimir force on graphene occur at separations significantly smaller compared to ordinary metals and dielectrics. At such small separations, the Casimir force is sufficiently strong to be measured experimentally. However, the presence of substrates to support the graphene significantly reduces the enhancement. We show theoretically that replacing the solid substrate beneath graphene with a thin dielectric membrane partially restores this strong thermal dependence. One of the interacting objects is a solid gold plate. The other object is a suspended dielectric membrane made of either 15 nm of silicon oxide or 13 nm silicon nitride, covered with graphene. At a separation of $\sim$500 nm, theoretical predictions yield changes in the Casimir pressure of up to 54 % and 40 % for silicon oxide and silicon nitride, respectively, when the temperature is increased from 10 K to 294 K. Measurements were performed for graphene on a suspended silicon nitride membrane at room temperature, using a gold-coated sphere attached to a cantilever as the force sensor. The measured force gradient is consistent with the theoretical prediction, although the thermal dependence could not be resolved, in part because of uncertainties in the optical properties of silicon nitride. Replacing a bulk substrate with a thin dielectric membrane covered with graphene provides a substantial reduction of the Casimir force, which may facilitate the stable operation of neutral nanomechanical elements at small separations.
summary: This research theoretically and experimentally investigates the Casimir force on graphene-coated suspended dielectric membranes. The key finding is that using a thin dielectric membrane instead of a bulk substrate significantly enhances the measurable thermal dependence of the Casimir force. This work is crucial for developing stable, highly sensitive nanomechanical devices by controlling long-range quantum forces.
main_problem: The paper investigates the Casimir force acting on thin dielectric membranes covered with graphene, with a specific focus on quantifying and understanding the thermal dependence of this force.
main_result: Theoretically, replacing a solid substrate beneath graphene with a thin dielectric membrane partially restores the strong thermal dependence of the Casimir force. Experimentally, measurements confirmed force gradients consistent with theory, although resolving the full thermal dependence was limited by material property uncertainties.
method: The study employs both theoretical calculations using the Lifshitz formalism and experimental force measurements using a resonant cantilever detector.
model_or_system: The system involves a solid gold plate interacting with a suspended dielectric membrane ($	ext{SiO}_2$ or $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$) coated with graphene. Theoretical models incorporate the graphene conductivity and the dielectric response of the supporting materials.
key_observables: Casimir pressure and force gradient ($F'$), and the change in force gradient when temperature increases from 10 K to 294 K.
important_parameters: Separation distance ($z \sim 500 	ext{ nm}$), Temperature ($T$), and the dielectric properties ($\epsilon(\omega)$) of $	ext{SiO}_2$ and $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$.
main_assumptions: The theoretical framework relies on the Lifshitz formalism and the Proximity Force Approximation (PFA). Experimental analysis assumes the membrane remains flat and relies on accurate optical characterization of the dielectric layers.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup, the measured force gradients comparing theory to experiment for both solid and suspended membranes, and the optical properties ($\epsilon'(\omega)$ and $\epsilon''(\omega)$) of the dielectric materials.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from theoretical modeling of the Casimir force using the Lifshitz formalism, detailing the role of graphene and the substrate. It then presents experimental measurements using a cantilever setup, comparing the measured force gradients on solid versus suspended membranes, and concludes by discussing the implications for nanomechanical stability.
why_interesting: This work bridges fundamental quantum electrodynamics (Casimir effect) with modern materials science (graphene, thin dielectrics) and nanomechanics, providing quantitative predictions for forces at the nanoscale that are relevant to quantum sensing and actuation.
